120	Grafting is not among the seven commandments
121	of the Torah, so it carries no death penalty.
122	It is forbidden, but the Torah did not impose death. That is why it is not
123	written in the Torah. This is the reason
124	that the Rambam writes that it is forbidden to them. Right? Forbidden
125	to them. What he is saying is, HaShem forbid,
126	that if it is done through a gentile, it is not right. Even
127	through a gentile it is forbidden, and not only that. Even if the
128	gentile transgressed and did it, and he did not hear our halachot, and he won't
129	listen to the Rambam, who is the Rambam to him, a nobody,
130	an idiot, a fool, would he understand the Rambam? He will not listen, he
131	will not know, he will not understand. But even if he transgressed
132	and did it, and this is found in a Jew's field, the Jew must
133	uproot this grafted tree,
134	this kilayim. It is forbidden to maintain it, and he is
135	maintaining kilayim indeed. It is forbidden.
136	So we say, since this is certainly not
137	desired by HaShem, that neither a Jew may graft
138	nor a gentile may graft, then certainly it is
139	not desired by HaShem. Therefore there is a correct reason
140	for what the Halachot Ketanot says, that by the letter of the law it is not
141	good to say Shehecheyanu. But certainly in all matters of
142	blessings we always follow the custom, what they were accustomed to do
143	according to the opinion of the great ones. We listen to the custom, we follow
144	the custom. And here in Jerusalem
145	several great ones testified, such as Rabbi Yosef Chaim,
146	in his book Birkei Yosef, and also Rabbi Eliyahu Mani in his book
147	Zecher Eliyahu, that in Jerusalem they were accustomed to say Shehecheyanu on
148	oranges, even though they are grafted, and this custom
149	still exists.
150	According to this, it is correct that we
151	rule like the Yaavetz regarding
152	Shehecheyanu, that one does bless.
153	But still, when we bless, it does not mean
154	that the words of the Halachot Ketanot are not correct. Indeed,
155	as he said, the prohibition of kilayim applies not only to Israel
156	but also to the sons of Noach, to the gentiles, as
157	the Rambam wrote. The Yaavetz thought
158	that there is no prohibition of kilayim for the sons of Noach. He followed
159	the Shach, Siftei Kohen, siman 297, ...
